topStories.headline: Cyberattack Breaches Heber City's Municipal Network; FBI Assisting Investigation
topStories.dek: An October 10 intrusion into city IT systems was contained within days, with no essential services interrupted, but a forensic investigation is ongoing.
topStories.body:
A cyberattack breached the Heber City Municipal Corporation's local IT network on Saturday, October 10, the city disclosed on October 15. City IT staff were alerted to the intrusion and, according to a city spokesperson, "took steps to stop and contain it expeditiously." Systems were reported fully back online and secure by Thursday, October 15, five days after the breach.

No essential city services were suspended during the incident. The city's public-facing website, heberut.gov, operates on a separate cloud-based platform and was unaffected throughout. The spokesperson confirmed that residents can use online bill pay and other services at heberut.gov "with full confidence."

The FBI is assisting in a forensic investigation to determine the scope and origin of the attack. The city has not publicly identified the affected internal systems or applications, disclosed whether municipal data was accessed or removed, or named a responsible group or method. Whether the attack involved ransomware has not been confirmed.

The breach comes at a busy moment for Heber City's local government, with a November 3 general election approaching and multiple county-level races on the ballot. City officials have not announced a timeline for the FBI investigation's completion or indicated when more information will be made public.

topStories.headline: Heber Valley Temple Walls Rising — but Utah Supreme Court's Final Word Still Months Away
topStories.dek: Construction is visibly advancing on the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' temple on East Center Street, even as attorneys wait for the high court to settle the underlying appeal.
topStories.body:
Basement walls are rising from an excavated pit on 18 acres along East Center Street in Heber City, making the Heber Valley Utah Temple one of the more visible construction projects in the valley — even as the Utah Supreme Court has yet to issue a final ruling on the legal challenge that has shadowed it for years.

The Utah Supreme Court heard oral arguments in the case on September 4. Attorney Robert Mansfield, who represents the group of Red Ledges residents who have opposed the temple from the start, said this week he would be surprised if an opinion is issued before the end of October and that a final decision could be another month or two away. The church and Wasatch County are proceeding with construction at their own risk: if the Supreme Court ultimately sides with the plaintiffs, the church would bear the cost of demolishing what has been built and restoring the site to its original condition.

Deputy County Attorney Jon Woodard, who has represented Wasatch County since the case began in Fourth District Court, said it would not be impossible to restore the site if the court rules against the project, describing such work as standard in the construction industry. The plaintiffs contend the county used an improper legislative development agreement to approve the 210-foot-tall, 88,000-square-foot structure. Church attorneys argue all proper processes were followed.

The Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that construction could resume while the appeal is considered, lifting an injunction that had previously halted the project for roughly five months. The court specified at that time that the church was proceeding at its own financial risk.

topStories.headline: State Funding Threat Against Wasatch County Fades — but Fight Over Developer-Town Law Heats Up at Legislature
topStories.dek: After the governor's housing adviser threatened to pull $2.1 million in annual road funds over a rejected housing project, state and county officials have patched things up — even as the Utah House speaker signals he's open to repealing the underlying development law Wasatch County opposes.
topStories.body:
A weeks-long standoff between Wasatch County and the state over housing policy and development authority reached a quieter phase this week, even as the underlying dispute moved closer to the Legislature. County Manager Dustin Grabau said the county's state funding — including roughly $2.1 million per year in B and C road money — is now secure, after state and county officials met in late August and state officials acknowledged their initial approach was not constructive.

The conflict began in mid-August, when the Wasatch County Council voted down a legislative development agreement for a 144-home project on Utah Trust Lands east of Heber City. Within days, Gov. Spencer Cox's senior housing adviser Steve Waldrip delivered a message to the Heber City Council warning that the county's state funding was "now at risk." The confrontation drew sharp reaction from residents who saw the threat as overreach.

Separately, a fight continues over Senate Bill 258, a 2024 law that allows up to three landowners in mostly undeveloped, unincorporated areas to petition to create a "preliminary municipality" — a mechanism that Wasatch County leaders say lets developers bypass local land-use authority. The Wasatch County Council approved a resolution in September calling on the Legislature to repeal the law. Developer Philo Development has applied to create a proposed community called Wasatch Highlands under SB258 on roughly 3,500 acres of privately owned land near the rejected trust-land project.

As reported on October 12 by Utah News Dispatch, Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz said he fully expects repeal or substantial changes to SB258 to be discussed when the Legislature convenes in January 2027. Gov. Cox has also left the door open to changes. Wasatch County says it remains open to housing solutions better suited to local conditions, including a potential land swap for the trust-land parcel.

moreNews.headline: Sheriff Says He Won't Resign; County Council Weighs Options After Closed-Door Session
moreNews.body: Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby stated publicly this week that he has no plans to resign following his felony indictment on obstruction of justice charges connected to the Kouri Richins murder case. The county council met in a closed session on October 13 to discuss what officials described only as the "character, professional competence, or physical or mental health of an individual," without naming Rigby. After the session, council members told KUTV they are open to the sheriff voluntarily taking administrative leave, but County Manager Dustin Grabau acknowledged there are "very few remedies in state code" to compel action against an elected official. The Bureau of Criminal Investigation has directed the county to revoke Rigby's access to certain privileged law enforcement information. His term expires December 31, 2026.

moreNews.headline: Mail-In Ballots Arrive; Early In-Person Voting Begins October 27
moreNews.body: Mail-in ballots for the November 3 general election were mailed to Wasatch County voters on October 13. The ballot includes races for Utah House District 59, Wasatch County Council Seats A, C, and F, Wasatch County Sheriff, county attorney, clerk-auditor, and school board seats. Voters not yet registered to vote by mail have until October 27 to request a ballot. Early in-person voting is available October 27 through 30, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Wasatch County Administration building.

moreNews.headline: Homestead Midway Utah Opens The Barn, a New 17,636-Square-Foot Event Venue
moreNews.body: Homestead Midway Utah debuted The Barn at Homestead this week, a new 17,636-square-foot event venue on the resort's nearly 190-acre property in Midway. The venue, designed for weddings, retreats, and milestone celebrations, is part of the resort's multi-phase transformation. It includes a Carriage House with private green rooms and a newly constructed Mountain View Deck with panoramic valley views. The resort is located at 700 North Homestead Drive in Midway.
